lines.text: Chapter one, section four. Geometric growth and bet sizing.
When Ivan has a truly polarized range, the way to squeeze the most money out of his Aces is not to guess a bet size, it is to grow the pot geometrically.
Geometric growth means picking a bet size on the current street such that if the pot doubles or triples according to that ratio on every street, the last bet is exactly all-in.
In our two-street game with three dollars behind and a two-dollar pot, that works out to a one-dollar turn bet followed by a two-dollar all-in on the river.
In a deep-stacked version of the same game with eight dollars behind, geometric growth means a two-dollar full-pot turn bet followed by a six-dollar all-in on the river.
The general rule is: same fraction of the pot on every street, ending with the entire stack in the pot.

You can prove that this maximizes the expected value of a perfectly polarized range using calculus, but the intuition is that the bet-to-pot ratio is what determines how many bluffs your opponent must call, and keeping that ratio constant balances value and pressure across streets.
This is why an off-the-cuff turn bet like check-min-bet then jam plays badly against a solid opponent; the min-bet does not build the pot enough to make the river shove threatening.
In real poker, hands are almost never perfectly polarized, so geometric growth is a starting heuristic, not a strict rule.

But when you have a hand at the top of your range on the turn and you plan to bet the river, ask yourself: does this bet size let me shove the river naturally, or am I stranding myself with an awkward jam?
Getting the ratio roughly right on the turn is one of those small decisions that quietly makes you more money on every polarized runout for the rest of your career.
